title: A poet's lament
hookLine: Amrita Pritam wrote a lament for Punjab's daughters in 1947

lines: TODAY I CALL ON WARIS SHAH.
cards: A young woman, a refugee herself, born into a Sikh family in a town that is now in Pakistan. Her name is Amrita Pritam. In 1947, with Punjab torn in two, she writes a poem.
It doesn't call on a politician or a general. It calls on a poet who has been dead a very long time, a Muslim Sufi named Waris Shah, who wrote the old Punjabi love story of Heer and Ranjha.
Her first line, in Punjabi, is a summons: today I call on Waris Shah. Why would a grieving Sikh woman call to a Muslim poet in his grave?

teach.b: First, who she calls. Waris Shah wrote Heer, the long poem of a young woman of Punjab, her lover, and the sorrow that came to her. It's a story Punjabis of different faiths share.

So Amrita Pritam goes to him as the poet who once wrote down the pain of one daughter of Punjab. Second, what she asks. In her poem, when one daughter of Punjab wept, Waris Shah wrote a whole tale of grief.

Now the daughters of Punjab are weeping, and she asks him to speak from among the graves and turn the next page of his book of love. She speaks of poison mixed into the waters of Punjab, and of blood across its land.
Third, what she doesn't do. The poem names no enemy. It doesn't ask for revenge, and it doesn't sort the dead into ours and theirs.

teach.h: ONE DAUGHTER THEN, THE DAUGHTERS NOW.
teach.b: The daughters in it are simply Punjab's daughters.
It's a lament, a mourning song, and it holds the whole land at once. Fourth, an older bridge. Sikhs don't have to look outside their own scripture for a Muslim poet of Punjab.

teach.h: FARID'S VERSES IN THE GURU GRANTH SAHIB.
teach.b: The Guru Granth Sahib keeps the Punjabi verses of Sheikh Farid, a Sufi, alongside the hymns of the Gurus; you met his verses earlier in this block, at Nankana and at Jaito.
A Sikh-born poet reaching across faiths to a Sufi was walking a road Punjab already knew. In a year of knives, someone picked up a pen and grieved for everyone.

how: Amrita Pritam's poem to Waris Shah is read and sung by Punjabis remembering Partition, and the Guru Granth Sahib keeps the Punjabi verses of the Sufi Sheikh Farid alongside the Gurus' hymns.

games.q: you're a young poet in 1947, and Punjab is torn in two. who do you call on in your poem?
o: a general, to avenge the dead.
Waris Shah, the old Sufi poet of Heer.
games.why: Amrita Pritam calls on Waris Shah to speak from among the graves and write the new grief of Punjab's daughters.

practice: Bring to mind one sorrow in the world right now, near or far, and hold it the way the poem does: without naming an enemy, without choosing sides among the grieving. Breathe in and let it be heavy; breathe out and let it be shared.
If you pray, let Waheguru hold it with you.
